claims.text: Adding a small, controlled amount of ZrC to a CrMnFeCoNi HEA bond coat will improve its long-term durability and reliability.
The durability improvement will result from enhanced oxidation resistance and mechanical integrity.
A conventional CrMnFeCoNi HEA coating without ceramic reinforcement is an appropriate untreated baseline.
Approximately 4 wt% ZrC is an optimized addition level for the HEA feedstock.
The added ZrC will disperse uniformly within the alloy matrix during coating synthesis.
The modified bond coat should remain effective during cyclic exposure in air up to about 900°C.
Uniformly dispersed ZrC particles form a secondary phase in the HEA matrix.
The ZrC secondary phase acts as a barrier to diffusion.
The ZrC secondary phase impedes crack propagation.
ZrC has sufficient thermodynamic stability at elevated temperature to limit outward diffusion of reactive elements.
Limiting reactive-element diffusion suppresses formation of non-protective oxides.
ZrC reinforces the HEA microstructure by hindering crack initiation and propagation under cyclic thermal stress.
Relative to the untreated bond coat, the ZrC-modified coating will have a slower oxidation rate.
Relative to the untreated bond coat, the ZrC-modified coating will retain its mechanical properties better.
Relative to the untreated bond coat, the ZrC-modified coating will have improved adhesion reliability during thermal cycling.
An effective ZrC-content range is approximately 2–5 wt%.
ZrC contents above the proposed optimal range may cause excessive brittleness or processing complications.
Uniform ZrC dispersion is necessary to avoid localized weaknesses.
ZrC addition has been shown to improve the corrosion resistance of CrMnFeCoNi HEA coatings in concentrated NaCl solution and is promising for oceanic environments.
Failure to obtain statistically significant improvements in oxidation, mechanical stability, and adhesion, or observation of increased brittleness, would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The intervention describes adding ZrC to the feedstock, implying pre-existing ZrC reinforcement, whereas the structural mediator calls the particles an in situ formation. The synthesis route does not explain how added ZrC is newly formed in situ.
